phase1.intro:
CSV — comma-separated values — is one of the simplest, most common formats for moving tabular data between programs.

Where do you want to start?

topics.buttonText: How do I read and write a basic CSV file?
dialogue: Writing one is straightforward: a BufferedWriter, a header line written first, then one write() + newLine() pair per record. Reading follows the same shape in reverse — a BufferedReader, skip (or capture) the header, then loop with readLine() and split on the comma.
`line.split(",")` hands you back an array of the individual field values as Strings, which you then parse into the actual types you need.

stickyNote.definition: Writing CSV: header line + write()/newLine() per record. Reading: readLine() + line.split(",") to get an array of field Strings.

topics.buttonText: Why does naive comma-splitting sometimes break?
dialogue: [[warn:Naive comma-splitting breaks the instant a field legitimately CONTAINS a comma]]. `"Alice, Smith"` as a single quoted field looks, to a plain split(","), like TWO separate fields — split() doesn't understand quoting at all.
[[key:For genuinely correct CSV parsing — quoted fields, escaped quotes, embedded newlines — reach for a real CSV library]] like OpenCSV or Apache Commons CSV.

stickyNote.definition: Naive split(",") breaks on fields containing a comma, even if quoted — real CSV parsing needs a library like OpenCSV, not hand-rolled splitting.

topics.buttonText: What should I check before indexing a split() result?
dialogue: [[key:Always check the array length after split() before indexing into it]] — a malformed or short row can hand you back fewer elements than expected, and reaching for `parts[3]` on a 2-element array throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

stickyNote.definition: A malformed CSV row can produce a shorter array than expected — check the array's length before indexing to avoid ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

phase1.openingDialogue: CSV is simple tabular text — but naive comma-splitting breaks on quoted fields, and skipping length checks invites a crash. 📊

phase2.errorMessage:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 1 out of bounds for length 1
    at Test.main(Test.java:9)
phase2.explanation:
parts[1] assumes every line has at least 2 comma-separated fields — and this particular line apparently doesn't, so split(",") handed back a shorter array than expected. Reaching for parts[1] on an array that doesn't have an index 1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

This is a genuinely common CSV problem, and it has a few different real causes: an empty field can shrink the split in surprising ways, a stray trailing comma changes the count, and — the trickiest one — a properly quoted field that legitimately contains a comma, like "Alice, Smith", will get split() into two fake fields instead of the one real one it's supposed to be.

[[key:always check parts.length before indexing into a split() result]]: if (parts.length >= 2) { ... } else { System.out.println("Skipping malformed line: " + line); }. And for real production CSV handling, [[warn:a hand-rolled split(",") genuinely isn't enough]]; that's when a real CSV parsing library earns its keep.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a row doesn't have as many fields as expected~

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's write and parse a tiny CSV file together~

mcq.question:
What's the main risk of parsing CSV with a plain line.split(",")?

A) It runs too slowly on large files
B) It doesn't correctly handle a comma that appears inside a quoted field
C) It can't read files larger than 1MB
D) It only works with numeric data

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates a CSV file called "employees.csv" with header: ID,Name,Department,Salary
2. Writes 4 employee records to the file
3. Reads the file back
4. Calculates and prints the average salary
5. Prints all employees in the "IT" department

Use BufferedReader/BufferedWriter for file I/O.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: CSV has never actually had one single official standard — RFC 4180 (2005) is the closest thing to a formal specification, but it came decades after CSV was already in widespread use, which is a big part of why real-world CSV files vary so much in exactly how they handle quoting, line endings, and delimiters.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
